analysis.one_liner: Strips accelerated tax depreciation from power plants earning returns above 15 percent.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee in June 2001 and never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote, dying there when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would deny the accelerated depreciation tax break to any electric generating facility earning a pretax return above 15 percent in a year, and would claw back the extra tax benefits such a facility had already claimed. Facilities using wind, solar, or water power would be exempt. The stated purpose is to stop power plant owners from collecting both excess profits and special tax incentives at the same time.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers and electricity customers. When a power plant earns outsized profits, the bill would end the faster tax write-offs that let the owner shelter that income, recovering earlier benefits as taxable income. During periods of high electricity prices, the measure would take back a subsidy from generators profiting at consumers' expense.

how_it_helps.text: A facility with a pretax rate of return above 15 percent for the year would lose accelerated depreciation and would have to include previously claimed accelerated benefits in gross income, recapturing the tax advantage [S3].

The CRS summary states the bill denies accelerated depreciation and recaptures previously permitted accelerated benefits for facilities with excess profits, defined as a pretax return above 15 percent [S2].

Facilities producing electricity from renewable sources — wind, sun, or water power — are explicitly exempted, so the provision targets high-profit conventional generation rather than clean energy [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Electric generating companies whose facilities clear the 15 percent return threshold. They would face slower depreciation schedules going forward and a one-time tax recapture of accelerated benefits already claimed, increasing their tax bills in high-profit years.

drawbacks.text: The 15 percent pretax return threshold is a blunt trigger: a facility whose returns spike in a single year — because of a fuel-price shock, a shortage, or one good contract — would lose the deduction and face recapture even if its long-run returns were normal [S3].

The bill requires calculating a separate rate of return for each facility, allocating debt and income to individual plants and imputing prices for sales to related companies, a compliance burden that tax administrators and generators would have to police and contest [S3].

Raising the tax cost of owning generation exactly when returns are high could reduce incentives to build or keep capacity online during shortages, when new supply is most needed — a cost an honest supporter would have to weigh against the revenue recovered [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core idea is straightforward — companies should not collect both outsized profits and accelerated tax write-offs — and the recapture mechanism recovers real money. But the design is crude: a single-year 15 percent return test can penalize volatile-but-unremarkable businesses, and the facility-by-facility accounting it requires is complicated to administer. A narrower trigger or a multi-year averaging rule would have addressed those objections. As written, the bill trades some risk of overreach for a direct clawback from the most profitable generators.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Ways and Means Committee, which never acted on it, so it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Jim McDermott introduced the bill on June 6, 2001 [S1].
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means [S5].
The committee took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — and the bill expired with the 107th Congress on January 3, 2003 [S5].
The bill attracted only two cosponsors: the House's sole Independent member and one of its 208 Democrats [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Owners of highly profitable electric generating facilities, who kept both their excess profits and their accelerated tax depreciation because the bill never advanced.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so no partisan split is on the record; support was limited to the Democratic sponsor, one House Democrat, and the House's single Independent, with no Republicans involved.

industries.industry: Investor-owned electric generating companies and utilities
industries.note: The bill would strip accelerated depreciation from any facility earning more than a 15 percent pretax return and claw back benefits already claimed, raising their taxes in exactly the years they profit most. Their interest in keeping those write-offs runs against ratepayers and taxpayers, since the subsidy compounds high prices with a tax shelter [S3].

The bill explicitly exempts facilities using wind, sun, or water power, so renewable generators keep their depreciation benefits regardless of profits. That gives them a relative tax advantage over conventional generators, aligning with the bill's push toward cleaner sources [S3].
